channel.title: Exoplanet Papers | Daily arXiv Summaries
channel.description: Daily summaries of exoplanet research papers from arXiv astro-ph.EP, written for general audiences.

item.title: Systematic Uncertainties in Rocky Exoplanet Reflected Light from Incomplete Laboratory BRDF Measurements
item.dc:creator: Leonardos Gkouvelis et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Astronomers have started studying rocky planets outside our solar system, and they want to know what those planets' surfaces are made of. Is it dark basalt, pale sand, or something else? Reading a surface from a distance is like identifying a fabric from across a room. To do it, scientists compare a planet's light with laboratory measurements of rocks and minerals. But most of those lab measurements were taken from just one lighting and viewing angle. That is like judging a satin sheet by a single photograph, when its shine changes as you walk around it. What They Did The researchers asked what goes wrong when a lab spectrum comes from only one angle. They tested whether different combinations of the settings that describe how a surface scatters light could all match the same single-angle spectrum. They then used each combination to predict what a distant planet would look like. The predictions covered how brightness changes across the planet's phases, how reflective the planet is overall, and how bright it appears next to its star. They worked at wavelengths from 0.5 to 1.7 micrometres, the range future space telescopes such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) are expected to target. They also checked the common shortcut of assuming light scatters equally in all directions. Finally, they used measurements taken at many angles from the Bloomsburg University Goniometer dataset. Key Findings Many different combinations of settings reproduced the same single-angle spectrum yet predicted different angular behavior. That produced large uncertainties in the predicted signals, especially at small phase angles, when the planet is nearly fully lit as seen from Earth. The simple equal-scattering assumption can also bias the results. When the multi-angle measurements were used, the uncertainty collapsed. Looking Forward The study argues that reliable models of rocky exoplanet light need laboratory measurements taken from many angles, not just one. Building such datasets would let future telescopes interpret planetary surfaces with much more confidence.

item.title: Solar System Surface Technosignatures: Searching for Signs of Artificial Design on Extraterrestrial Terrain
item.dc:creator: Ana Henrique, Sofia Sheikh, Benjamin Fields
item.description: Why It Matters For decades, the hunt for alien technology has mostly meant listening for radio signals, like sitting by a radio hoping to catch a distant station. But broadcasts are fleeting, and a civilization might transmit for only a short window. This paper argues for a complementary idea: look for lasting marks on the ground. Think of the pyramids, ancient roads, or giant earthworks on Earth, which outlast the people who built them. On quiet worlds like the Moon and Mars, where little geological activity erases the surface, artificial patterns could stay visible for hundreds of millions of years. What They Did This is a proposal, not an observing campaign. The authors borrow an anthropological lens, the way archaeologists read human-shaped landscapes, to define "surface technosignatures": non-random, intentional patterns on planetary terrain. They point to two recent developments that make the search timely. One is extremely sharp imagery, such as pictures from the HiRISE (High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment) camera on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. The other is machine-learning methods that are good at anomaly detection, meaning spotting things that look out of place. Key Findings The paper does not report a discovery. Its main outcome is a roadmap with two possible ways to build an AI model for the search. A supervised approach would learn from labeled examples, like teaching a child to recognize cats from photos. An unsupervised approach would learn what ordinary terrain looks like and flag whatever doesn't fit. Flagged spots could then be checked with complementary tools: LiDAR (laser-based 3D mapping), ground-penetrating radar, and reflectance spectroscopy, which reads a surface's makeup from how it reflects light. Looking Forward The authors say these methods would allow the first quantitative upper limits on surface technosignatures. Even if nothing is found, scientists could state firmly how much, if anything, could be hiding in the terrain searched so far. The work would also bring side benefits for planetary science, since tools that find the unusual could help study odd natural features on other worlds.

item.title: OGLE-2013-BLG-1125/MOA-2013-BLG-584: Discovery of a gas giant orbiting an M dwarf
item.dc:creator: E. Bachelet et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Giant planets like Saturn and Jupiter are thought to need a lot of raw material to form. Small, dim stars called M dwarfs, the most common kind in our galaxy, have less material around them, so finding a big planet circling one is a puzzle. Each new example helps astronomers test their ideas about how planets are built. So far, the list of giant planets around such small stars is short. What They Did The team used a technique called gravitational microlensing. When one star drifts almost exactly in front of a more distant star, its gravity acts like a natural magnifying glass and briefly brightens the background star. If the foreground star has a planet, the planet adds a small extra blip to that brightening. This event, named OGLE-2013-BLG-1125/MOA-2013-BLG-584, was watched by two survey projects, OGLE (Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment) and MOA (Microlensing Observations in Astrophysics). Follow-up telescopes from Las Cumbres Observatory (LCO), the Microlensing Follow-Up Network (μFUN), and Mindstep also contributed. The researchers built a computer model of how the brightness rose and fell over time. They also used data from the Keck II telescope, collected in 2018, to add further constraints on the lensing system. Key Findings The model points to a planet with a mass of 105 ± 13 times the mass of Earth. That is similar to Saturn, which weighs in at roughly 95 Earths. The star it orbits is very light, at 0.139 ± 0.011 times the mass of our Sun, or about one-seventh of it. The system lies about 1.00 ± 0.08 kiloparsecs from us, which is roughly 3,300 light-years. Looking Forward This discovery adds one more entry to the small collection of giant planets known around low-mass stars. Such systems provide constraints on theories of planet formation. As more of them are found, astronomers can better judge how often small stars manage to build large planets, and which formation ideas hold up.

item.title: Radio and high-energy variable emission from a multi-wavelength follow-up of the infant planet-hosting star V1298 Tau
item.dc:creator: M. Damasso et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Planets are born around young stars, and young stars can be rough neighbours. V1298 Tau is a very young, magnetically active star, a bit cooler than the Sun, that hosts several planets. That makes it a benchmark for studying how planetary systems form and change in their earliest stages. The star's magnetic storms, flares and radiation shape the environment its planets live in. Understanding the star's behaviour is therefore part of understanding the planets' history. What They Did Between 2025 and 2026, the team watched the star in several "colours" of light. The Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA), a radio telescope, observed it at 4.5–6.5 gigahertz over repeated visits. The Swift satellite tracked X-rays and near-ultraviolet light for 20 days, ending one month before the radio campaign began. The team compared these data with a publicly available optical brightness record from the ASAS-SN survey, which follows the star's brightness as it spins. Key Findings Radio emission turned up in 90% of the visits. It switched between a bright state (at or above 0.1 millijansky per beam) and a faint one within days or even hours. The radio signal was moderately linked to the optical brightness, which hints that it rises and falls with the star's rotation. Except in one visit, there were no rapid changes over minutes and no sign of circularly polarised radio waves. Overall, the radio signal fits electrons spiralling in magnetic fields in the star's hot outer atmosphere, the corona. The X-ray output varied between 1.2 and 2.5 × 10³⁰ erg per second. The team also caught the fading phase of a stellar flare and found evidence that the X-rays track the optical light. Finally, V1298 Tau follows the Güdel-Benz relation, a nearly straight-line link between a star's radio and X-ray brightness. Looking Forward These results tie the star's radio and high-energy flickering to its magnetic activity, and they show it behaves like other active stars. The X-ray and radio observations were separated by about a month, so they could not be compared moment by moment. Observing a young planet-hosting star in all these bands at the same time would give a sharper picture of its stormy surroundings.

item.title: White dwarf pollution in wide binaries I: the effects of stellar evolution
item.dc:creator: Constanza Norambuena, Carolina Charalambous, Claudia Aguilera-Gómez
item.description: Why It Matters When a star like our Sun runs out of fuel, it swells up, sheds much of its material, and leaves behind a dense, Earth-sized ember called a white dwarf. Many white dwarfs have dust and metals such as iron and silicon in their thin outer layers. These elements should sink out of sight quickly, so astronomers think the white dwarfs are still "eating" rocky debris, probably leftovers from planets and asteroids that once circled them. That makes white dwarfs a way to study the building blocks of distant planetary systems. Many of these stars also have a distant stellar companion, so a key question is what pushes the rocky material inward: the aging star itself, or the pull of its companion? What They Did The researchers built computer simulations, using a tool called REBOUND that tracks how objects move under gravity. They modelled a wide pair of stars in which one star hosts a Jupiter-mass planet and a belt of small rocky bodies called planetesimals. To follow the star's changes, they used detailed stellar life-story models from a code called MESA (Modules for Experiments in Stellar Astrophysics). They tried two versions of how the star loses mass as it ages, and they varied the size and shape of the binary orbit. The simulations ran up to the white dwarf stage and included tidal effects. Key Findings The choice of mass-loss history had only a minor effect on whether the planet survived. It mainly changed the timing and efficiency of rocky material reaching the white dwarf. The layout of the binary mattered much more. Wider binaries delivered rocky material to the white dwarf at the highest rates, which fits the observation that polluted white dwarfs are common in wide binaries. The reservoirs of planetesimals also lasted a long time, and they lasted longer in wider binaries. That could allow metal pollution to continue for billions of years. Looking Forward This is the first paper in a series, and it points to the companion star's orbit as the main driver of pollution. The simulations used one planet and one disc, so future work can test more varied planetary systems.

item.title: The Pandora SmallSat: Target Selection and Early Science
item.dc:creator: Emily A. Gilbert et al.
item.description: Why It Matters When a planet passes in front of its star, some starlight filters through the planet's atmosphere and carries chemical fingerprints. Stars are not smooth, though. They have dark spots and bright patches, a bit like freckles that come and go, and these can mimic or hide a planet's signal. Telescopes can mistake a star's moods for a planet's air. Learning to separate the two is essential if we want to read the atmospheres of faraway worlds correctly. What They Did Pandora is a small satellite, or "smallsat," chosen in the first group of NASA's Pioneers missions. It measures a star's brightness in visible light while also splitting near-infrared light into its colors (spectroscopy). Watching both at once helps tell star effects from planet effects. The team picked 20 main targets. Each gets 10 separate transit observations, and each observation lasts 24 hours. All the planets orbit K and M dwarfs, which are cooler and smaller than our Sun. The stars were chosen to span different spin rates and activity levels. Key Findings This paper mainly describes how the targets were chosen. The abstract does not report specific scientific results. The planets range from 1.5 to 15 times Earth's radius and circle their stars every 1.7 to 11.5 days. Pandora also observes extra targets to fill gaps in its schedule. These include young star systems, planets whose transit times shift slightly, brown dwarfs (objects between planets and stars), and planets whose brightness changes as they orbit. The authors say early results are discussed in the full paper, but the abstract gives no details. Looking Forward If the mission is extended, Pandora could take on more science. The authors outline possible options for that extended phase. As the observations continue, they should show how well Pandora can separate starlight quirks from true planetary atmospheres.
